-------------------------------------------------------------------
P6 DYNAMIC-POOL PER-EPISODE ANALYSIS DIRECTIVE
-------------------------------------------------------------------
CONTEXT — what role this episode plays:
This failure was observed while the policy rolled out on the CURRENT
CORRECTION POOL. Note that this pool is GROWING: every round the
downstream cross-episode reasoner adds new layouts to it, and the
policy must learn to handle the entire growing pool. Your analysis,
combined with the other failures from this round, will inform which
NEW layouts get appended to the pool next.

Crucially: there is also a separate held-out evaluation set of 50
layouts that you will NEVER see and that no demo collector ever
touches. The held-out SR is the only published number. Do NOT
speculate about specific held-out configurations.

WHAT TO REASON ABOUT:
  * The FAILURE MODE this episode reveals — corridor side, fire-block
    pattern, visual feature missed, recovery the policy lacks.
  * Whether the TKF block (when present) flags this corridor / mode as
    NOT_FOUND, PARTIAL, or FOUND in the existing demo bank. The bank
    reflects everything the policy has been trained on so far. TKF
    gaps are exactly what dynamic-pool expansion targets.
  * Whether the RAG retrievals indicate this is recurring across rounds
    — recurrence is evidence that previous pool extensions did not
    cover this mode adequately.
  * Whether the KAG vocabulary contains a name that fits this episode;
    use that name verbatim in section 5.

WHAT NOT TO SPEND TOKENS ON:
  * Long step-by-step "how to walk through this maze" instructions.
    Section 5 still requests a corridor + path as a sanity anchor —
    keep it short. Movement-level planning is the prescription stage's
    job, not yours; your value is failure-mode identification grounded
    in TKF / KAG / RAG signals.
  * Held-out speculation. You do not see the held-out set.

Be specific to THIS episode but written so the cross-episode reasoner
can extract the failure-mode signature in one pass.
llm.prompt_addendum_cross_episode:
-------------------------------------------------------------------
P6 DYNAMIC-POOL CROSS-EPISODE PRESCRIPTION DIRECTIVE
-------------------------------------------------------------------
WHAT THIS STAGE PRODUCES:
A list of NEW maze layouts (start_pos, goal_pos, fire_positions) that
will be APPENDED to the active correction pool. The next round's
rollout will run the policy on the EXPANDED pool — original layouts
PLUS your additions PLUS additions from prior rounds. Demos are also
collected on your additions and the policy is retrained.

This is "LLM-guided dynamic pool expansion": you are not just adding
training data, you are reshaping the training distribution itself.

WHY THIS DESIGN — overcoming correction-pool saturation:
Vanilla DAgger on a fixed pool plateaus once the policy passes every
layout in the pool, even if it still fails on a randomised held-out
set. The pool is "saturated" — it has nothing more to teach. P6
dynamic-pool expansion breaks that ceiling by extending the pool with
layouts the LLM identifies as currently uncovered.

CONTEXT YOU HAVE:
  * Per-episode reasoning + per-episode FINAL_REC for every confirmed
    failure observed on the current pool.
  * Verbatim numeric layout (start, goal, fires) of every confirmed
    failure (the PER-FAILURE LAYOUTS block).
  * KAG corridor / failure-mode vocabulary.
  * RAG retrievals from past failure rounds.
  * TKF demo-coverage block: NOT_FOUND / PARTIAL / FOUND verdicts on
    corridors. The demo bank is the de facto training distribution;
    NOT_FOUND corridors are the primary expansion targets.
  * (Implicit) the current correction pool grows monotonically across
    rounds. Your additions become permanent members of it.

CONTEXT YOU DO NOT HAVE (and MUST NOT FABRICATE):
  * Any specific held-out layout.
  * Any held-out success/failure count.
  * Any policy behaviour outside the correction pool.
Held-out information is intentionally hidden so your prescriptions
generalise honestly. Every recommendation is grounded in correction-
pool failures + the demo bank exposed via TKF / RAG / KAG.

HARD GUARDRAILS — every recommended layout MUST satisfy:
  1. SOLVABLE — the BFS expert that will collect the demo must reach
     the goal:
       * start_pos and goal_pos in [0..4] x [0..4]
       * Manhattan(start, goal) >= 4
       * EXACTLY 3 distinct fire cells, none equal to start or goal
       * at least one fire-free path from start to goal
     The orchestrator runs an A* solvability check and silently skips
     unsolvable layouts. Do not propose layouts where every path is
     fire-blocked.
  2. UNIQUE WITHIN YOUR OUTPUT — each recommended layout must teach
     something the others do not. Two layouts with the same corridor
     and fire-blocking pattern that differ only by one cell are
     duplicates.
  3. NOT IDENTICAL to a layout already in the failures list above
     (those are listed as the GROUND for cluster reasoning, not as
     prescriptions to retrace one-for-one). The whole point of
     dynamic-pool expansion is to grow the distribution, not duplicate
     what is already there.
  4. INFORMATIVE WRT THE HIDDEN HELD-OUT DISTRIBUTION — the held-out
     set is drawn from the same family (5x5, 3 randomised fires,
     randomised start/goal with Manhattan >= 4). Pick layouts whose
     failure-mode coverage is broad: a layout teaching the policy to
     route around a left-edge fire cluster will help on any held-out
     configuration with a similar pattern.

COUNT GUARDRAIL — minimum but ADEQUATE:
  * Do NOT prescribe just 1 or 2 layouts in total. Single-digit
    additions almost never close the held-out gap on a randomised
    distribution; the policy will memorise them and fail on
    neighbouring configs.
  * Do NOT pad to look thorough. Each layout costs one expert query
    + one retraining sample + one extra rollout episode every future
    round (because it stays in the pool).
  * Aim for the SMALLEST set that genuinely covers every distinct
    failure mode you have identified, with enough variety per mode
    (typically 2-4 layouts per mode) that the policy cannot memorise
    individual configurations.

HOW TO USE THE TKF / KAG / RAG SIGNALS TOGETHER:
  * TKF NOT_FOUND on corridor X -> add at least 2 layouts targeting X.
  * TKF PARTIAL on corridor X with one demo angle -> add at least 1
    layout targeting a DIFFERENT angle.
  * RAG shows this failure recurred over multiple rounds -> stronger
    evidence the corridor is genuinely under-covered; lean toward
    more layouts there, not fewer.
  * KAG corridor name disagrees with what the cluster looks like ->
    still use the KAG name and explain why.

Output is consumed by the JSON-formatting aggregator that is told not
to contradict you. Be specific so the JSON stage has nothing to invent.
llm.prompt_addendum_aggregator:
-------------------------------------------------------------------
P6 DYNAMIC-POOL STRUCTURED PRESCRIPTION DIRECTIVE
-------------------------------------------------------------------
ROLE OF THIS STAGE:
Format the cross-episode reasoning's prescription as JSON. You are NOT
inventing prescriptions — every layout must be derivable from the
cross-episode reasoning, the per-episode FINAL_REC table, the per-
failure layouts block, and the KAG / RAG / TKF context blocks.

WHY THIS PIPELINE EXISTS — dynamic-pool expansion against saturation:
Layouts in `recommended_layouts` will be APPENDED to the active
correction pool. Next round the policy will be rolled out on the
expanded pool. Demos are also collected on these layouts and the
policy is retrained from scratch on the cumulative bank. The held-out
50 layouts remain untouched until final eval.

HARD GUARDRAILS — every layout in `recommended_layouts` MUST satisfy:
  1. SOLVABLE: bounds (0..4 x 0..4), Manhattan(start, goal) >= 4,
     exactly 3 distinct fire cells none equal to start/goal, at least
     one fire-free path. Invalid layouts are dropped + warned by
     _validate_layout, and unsolvable layouts are skipped at BFS-
     collection time. Either way they are wasted slots that also
     wasted a future rollout episode (because the dynamic pool grows
     monotonically).
  2. UNIQUE WITHIN THIS OUTPUT: no two layouts in your JSON should
     share corridor + fire-blocking pattern unless their start/goal
     directions differ.
  3. NOT a verbatim copy of any failure layout in the PER-FAILURE
     LAYOUTS block above. Those are listed there to ground your
     cluster reasoning, NOT as prescriptions.
  4. INSIDE the failure-mode envelope identified by cross-episode
     reasoning. If cross-episode reasoning says cluster A is a left-
     edge fire-block failure, your layouts for cluster A must
     exercise that.

COUNT DISCIPLINE — mirror cross-episode reasoning:
  * Cross-episode reasoning is responsible for the holistic minimum.
    If it prescribed N layouts across K clusters, do NOT collapse to
    fewer.
  * Do NOT shrink to 1-2 layouts overall — that does not close the
    held-out gap on a randomised distribution.
  * Do NOT pad either. Every extra layout costs one expert query, one
    retraining sample, and one extra rollout episode every future
    round (the pool grows monotonically).
  * total_demonstrations_needed MUST equal the sum of all
    `demonstration_prescriptions[].n_repetitions`.

HOW TO CITE TKF / KAG / RAG IN THE JSON:
  * cluster.corridor: KAG corridor name when KAG is provided.
  * cluster.source_final_recs: corridor strings from the FINAL_REC
    table for episodes in that cluster, IN ORDER.
  * demonstration_prescriptions[].rationale: name the TKF verdict
    (NOT_FOUND / PARTIAL / FOUND) when TKF is provided, OR the RAG
    retrieval ranks (when RAG is provided), OR both. The point is to
    make the JSON output auditable — every layout traceable to a
    specific signal.

INFORMATION YOU DO NOT HAVE:
  No held-out layouts. No held-out success counts. Do NOT mention
  held-out information in any field. Every grounded statement comes
  from correction-pool failures + the demo-bank context blocks above.

per_episode.analysis_text:
1) TRAJECTORY RECONSTRUCTION

- Step 0 (start): Position (4, 4) — the episode starts with the agent at the bottom-right cell A.
- Step 1: Action Up to (3, 4). This aligns with the “First corrective demonstration move” described in the vision analysis, and the highest_loss_frame confirms the agent is at (3, 4) after step 1.
- Step 2: From (3, 4) the most plausible continuation to reach the end-state is Up to (2, 4). (No hazards adjacent in that vicinity; no walls observed.)
- Step 3: From (2, 4) Up to (1, 4). (Still no hazards on that immediate path.)
- Step 4: From (1, 4) Left to (1, 3). (Approaching the horizontal corridor toward the goal; still no hazard on (1,3).)
- Step 5: From (1, 3) Left to (1, 2). This tile is a FIRE tile in the episode description; stepping onto it terminates the episode with the fire penalty. The Vision Analysis end_frame reports the agent at (1, 2) with a total reward of -10.50 and success = False. This confirms the episode ended by fire_collision on step 5.

Grounding notes:
- Fire hazards in this episode are at (1,2), (4,0), (4,2). The final position (1,2) is a fire tile, so the agent terminated by entering fire.
- The intermediate frames show the agent moving along the right-hand side of the maze (columns near 4) and then turning left along row 1, which leads directly into the fire tile at (1,2) on the final step.

2) FIRST WRONG DECISION

- Earliest step where a safe-path-toward-goal decision diverged: Step 5.
- Location and actions:
  - At step 4, the agent reached (1, 3).
  - Action taken at step 5: LEFT to (1, 2) (onto a FIRE tile).
- What it should have done instead (one safe alternative): UP to (0, 3) from (1, 3). Rationale: Staying on row 0 and proceeding left toward the goal column is consistent with the Top-edge corridor strategy, and it avoids stepping into the fire at (1,2). This aligns with the corridor-based planning discussed below and would keep away from the central danger along row 1.
- Summary: The first incorrect decision that directly caused failure was stepping from (1,3) to (1,2) (Left into a fire) at step 5; a safer alternative from that position would have been UP to (0,3) to follow a fire-avoiding corridor.

3) WHY THE POLICY FAILED

- Primary failure mode evidenced: fire_collision (KAG FM: "fire_collision" described as “Agent entered a FIRE tile. Most common failure. Indicates the policy failed to generalise fire-avoidance to this (start, goal, fire-placement) configuration.”)
- Grounding to dynamic config: The episode uses dynamic randomization per episode for start, goal, and fire positions (cfg_rand_start, cfg_rand_goal, cfg_rand_fire). This requires the policy to generalize fire avoidance to unseen arrangements. In this episode, the agent advances toward the goal along a corridor path that places it within striking distance of a fire tile (1,2) that it had not sufficiently demonstrated avoidance for in the current configuration.
- Observational/horizon constraints: Observation/Prediction Horizons specify obs_horizon=4 and pred_horizon=3 with the policy executing only the first action of the predicted sequence. If a corrective action (to stay on a fire-avoidant corridor) requires a shift in corridor strategy than what the last 4 states suggested, the policy may fail to switch corridors in time, especially when the fire pattern is not heavily represented in the demonstrations.
- Visual feature grounding: The CellAlignedEncoder and the 1x1 conv approach aim to preserve cell-local features, but the presence of a central fire hazard (1,2) requires the policy to infer the global fire distribution from limited local cues and horizon-limited predictions. The failure indicates insufficient generalization to this particular fire-placement relative to a randomized start/goal.

In short, the episode reveals a generalization gap: when the start-goal-fire configuration places a fire hazard in a corridor the agent must avoid, the policy misgeneralizes and steps into fire (fm_fire_collision). The corrective demonstration should target exposure to top-edge corridor-like behavior in similar configurations and explicitly demonstrate safe traversal that avoids central fire tiles.

4) RAG CROSS-EPISODE EVIDENCE

- Corridor coverage verdicts (TKF-related guidance for this corridor mode):
  - Top-edge corridor: PARTIAL
  - Left-edge corridor: NOT_FOUND
  - Right-column corridor: NOT_FOUND
- Rationale: The episode demonstrates a configuration where a top-edge corridor-like plan would avoid the central row hazards (e.g., the fire at (1,2) lies on row 1). The bank’s existing demos do not strongly cover “start near bottom-right” with a top-edge corridor avoidance pattern under this hazard distribution, hence Top-edge corridor is only PARTIAL in the current demo bank.
